input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Evidence-aware prompts, generation, and LaTeX assembly
input.section_summary: Provide the evidence-aware prompt templates and templates for JSON-constrained generation, rules for composing section outputs into a coherent manuscript, and the LaTeX + refs.bib assembly process (citation mapping, bib entry generation, and final consistency checks).

output:
This section describes the design and implementation details of our evidence-aware prompting pipeline, the JSON-constrained generation format for individual sections, and the rules used to assemble those section artifacts into a coherent LaTeX manuscript with a refs.bib file. All descriptions below are framed as design choices and procedural specifications used in our system; empirical evaluation of these choices appears in the Experiments and Results sections.

Overview of the generation pipeline
- Goal. Produce section-level outputs that (a) explicitly reference supporting evidence, (b) conform to a machine-readable schema amenable to automated validation and editing, and (c) compose deterministically into a LaTeX manuscript with a consolidated bibliography.
- High-level steps. For each scheduled section, the system (1) retrieves and ranks candidate evidence items, (2) constructs an evidence-injected prompt according to a template, (3) requests a JSON-constrained section output from the generator, (4) validates the JSON and runs lightweight evidence-consistency checks, and (5) stores the validated artifact for later assembly.

Evidence-aware prompt templates
- Template structure. Each prompt is divided into (i) a short, deterministic instruction block that defines the task and the JSON schema to be produced, (ii) an evidence block that enumerates retrieved items with provenance metadata, and (iii) a generation directive that constrains tone, length, and the requirement to attach citation anchors to factual claims.
- Minimal example (conceptual, placeholders shown in angle brackets):
  - Instruction block: ``You will generate a JSON object for section <SECTION_ID>. Follow the schema: fields {title, body, claims, inline_citations}. Each claim must be supported by one or more evidence items listed below. Do not invent facts; if you cannot support a claim, mark it as 'unsupported'.''
  - Evidence block: numbered entries of the form ``<EVIDENCE_INDEX>: <short_snippet> — provenance: {doc_id, page, byte_offset, retrieval_score}''. Include up to K top-ranked items; K is a tunable parameter.
  - Generation directive: ``Produce the JSON object. For each sentence that asserts a factual proposition, add an inline citation '@e<EVIDENCE_INDEX>' referring to the supporting evidence index. Keep expository text concise (target N–M sentences).''
- Design rationale. Explicit enumeration of evidence with indices encourages the model to anchor assertions to concrete provenance items rather than free-floating citations. Requiring a dedicated 'claims' list (see JSON schema below) makes it straightforward to audit which assertions have direct support.

JSON-constrained section outputs
- Required fields. Each section output is a JSON object containing at minimum:
  - title: string
  - body: string (human-readable paragraph(s) intended for inclusion in the manuscript)
  - claims: list of claim objects, where each claim object contains:
    - claim_id: string
    - text: string (single declarative sentence)
    - evidence_refs: list of evidence indices (integers referring to items in the prompt evidence block)
    - support_type: one of {``direct_quote'', ``paraphrase'', ``inference'', ``unsupported''} (design choice to encourage explicitness)
  - inline_citations: optional mapping from textual spans in body to evidence_refs (used for LaTeX citation placement)
  - metadata: provenance and generation-time information (retrieval timestamps, model version, prompt hash)
- Validation semantics. A produced JSON object must (a) parse under a strict schema, (b) include at least one claim per required subsection (when applicable), and (c) list non-empty evidence_refs for claims labeled other than ``unsupported''. Claims marked ``unsupported'' are acceptable but flagged for human review during downstream auditing.
- Example claim object (conceptual):
  - { ``claim_id'': ``c1'', ``text'': ``X reduces Y under conditions Z.'', ``evidence_refs'': [1,3], ``support_type'': ``paraphrase'' }

Automated validation and lightweight evidence-consistency checks
- Syntax and schema checks. First-pass checks verify valid JSON and the presence of required fields. Failures at this stage trigger automated repair attempts (for example: re-requesting the output with stricter schema enforcement) or fall back to human review if automated repair fails.
- Evidence presence checks. For each claim with support_type != ``unsupported'', the validator confirms that the referenced evidence indices exist in the evidence block provided to the model. Missing indices are treated as schema violations.
- Surface-level cross-checks. The system performs fast heuristics to detect obvious mismatches between claim text and evidence snippets, such as absence of shared key tokens or negation polarity mismatches. These checks are intentionally conservative (preferring false negatives over false positives) and are used only to flag claims for manual inspection rather than to make final judgments.
- Failure handling. When validation fails, the pipeline follows a predetermined escalation: (1) automated repair by re-prompting with clarifying instructions; (2) expand the retrieved evidence pool and re-run generation; (3) if repeated attempts fail, mark the section artifact as requiring human editing and record detailed diagnostic logs.

Rules for composing section outputs into a manuscript
- Citation canonicalization. Each evidence item used across sections is mapped to a canonical bibliographic entry candidate. The mapping preserves provenance metadata (document identifier, page, snippet) to enable later manual verification of the corresponding bibliographic record.
- Bib-entry generation. For evidence items that correspond to scholarly documents, the pipeline attempts to construct a minimal bib entry (author/title/year/source). When metadata is insufficient or ambiguous, the system emits a bib entry placeholder that includes provenance and a unique key, flagged for curator inspection.
- Inline citation mapping. The JSON inline_citations mapping is translated into LaTeX citation anchors. If a claim references multiple evidence indices, the assembler collapses these into a single bracketed citation list linked to their corresponding bib keys.
- Ordering and cross-section consistency. The assembler preserves section ordering determined by the section graph scheduler. It also checks for duplicate or conflicting bibliographic keys and enforces unique keys per distinct provenance record.

Auditability and machine-readable outputs
- Audit traces. Each generated section artifact carries explicit metadata tying claims to evidence indices and to the retrieved document identifiers. These traces enable automated computation of citation coverage (fraction of claims with at least one evidence_ref) and facilitate targeted manual review.
- Editable artifacts. Because sections are stored as structured JSON, downstream edits (automated or human) can be applied at the claim level (e.g., replacing an unsupported claim or adding evidence_refs) and then revalidated and reassembled without regenerating unrelated content.

Conservative design choices and limitations
- No implicit citation insertion. The pipeline enforces that every factual claim emitted by the generator is accompanied by an explicit evidence_refs list; the model is instructed not to introduce bibliographic assertions without supporting evidence in the prompt.
- Human-in-the-loop gates. For bib entries with incomplete metadata, or for claims flagged by consistency checks, the system requires human verification prior to finalizing the refs.bib file.
- Intended conservatism. These design decisions trade off some fluency and automation for stronger auditability and reduced risk of unsupported assertions.

Implementation notes and practical heuristics
- Evidence budget. In practice, prompts include a tunable top-K evidence list to bound prompt size; K is chosen based on retrieval quality and prompt token limits. Sections that remain under-supported after exhausting the budget are marked for targeted retrieval expansion.
- Prompt templates as immutable contracts. Prompt templates and the JSON schema are treated as immutable contracts between the scheduler, retriever, generator, and assembler; changes to these artifacts trigger a re-validation pass across all previously generated sections.
- Diagnostic outputs. Every generation run produces a compact diagnostic bundle including the prompt, evidence block, the raw generator output, the parsed JSON, validation results, and a short diff if repair attempts modified the output. These bundles are stored alongside the manuscript for reproducibility.

Summary
This section specified the prompt templates, the required JSON structure for section outputs, the validation and repair pipeline, and the deterministic assembly rules that produce a LaTeX manuscript and refs.bib. The emphasis throughout is on mandatory, explicit citation of evidence for each factual claim, schema-constrained generation to facilitate automated validation, and conservative escalation to human review when automated checks are insufficient. The Experiments and Discussion sections cover empirical evaluation of these practices and their observed trade-offs.
